title: Do toddlers and chimpanzees help others without a reward?
blurb: Scientists from the Max Planck Institute in Leipzig dropped things just out of reach. Toddlers and chimpanzees handed them back, even when they got nothing for it.

original.title: Spontaneous Altruism by Chimpanzees and Young Children
original.authors: Warneken, F., Hare, B., Melis, A. P., Hanus, D., and Tomasello, M.

cards.b: Many people thought only humans help others when there is nothing in it for them. Is that true? And is helping something we learn as we grow, or something even very young children do? Do our close cousins, the chimpanzees, help too?

Felix Warneken and Michael Tomasello studied how children and apes think at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany. Brian Hare, Alicia Melis and Daniel Hanus worked with them. They tested chimpanzees at a sanctuary on Ngamba Island in Uganda, and also young children. They published in 2007.

A grown-up the chimpanzees did not know reached for a stick he could not get. For the 18-month-old toddlers, it was a pencil on a table. Would they hand it over? Sometimes the helper got a reward, a piece of banana or a toy block. Sometimes they got nothing. In other tests, helping meant climbing up or stepping over soft toy snakes.

img.alt: Four simple plans of the test rooms, showing where the helper, the grown-up and the out-of-reach stick or pencil were.
img.credit: Figure 1, Warneken et al., PLOS Biology 2007, CC BY 4.0

cards.b: Both toddlers and chimpanzees handed over the object much more when the grown-up was reaching for it. They helped just as much with no reward as with a reward. In another test, a chimpanzee could open a door for another chimpanzee to reach food. Many did, by pulling a pin that freed a chain.

img.alt: A plan of three rooms joined by doors held shut with chains. One chimpanzee can free the chain so another can get in.
img.credit: Figure 4, Warneken et al., PLOS Biology 2007, CC BY 4.0

cards.b: The first test had 36 chimpanzees and 36 toddlers, which is a fair number. Toddlers often helped within the first 30 seconds. Chimpanzees helped too but were slower and needed more clues. Scientists still argue about how much chimpanzees care about others, so this is part of a bigger story.

Toddlers only one and a half years old helped a stranger without being asked or paid. So the wish to help may start very early, before children are taught to be kind. Chimpanzees share some of this. Helping may have deep roots, going back to a shared ancestor of humans and chimpanzees.

If there is a toddler in your family, try this with a parent watching. Fathima drops a peg while hanging clothes, and reaches for it, but cannot get it. She does not ask for help. Does the little one pick it up and give it to her? Next time she drops a peg on purpose. Does the toddler still help?

The toddlers helped even when they got no reward. Some people say a reward, like a sweet, makes children help more. Others say rewards spoil the good feeling of helping. What do you think? Why do you help someone when nobody is watching?

words.m: helping others even when you get nothing back
something nice you get for doing something
a safe home where rescued animals are looked after
a relative who lived long, long ago, before your grandparents' grandparents
